The Widow Douglas's generous hospitality was an irresistible temptation. Before long, that and Tom's persuasion won the argument. They agreed to tell no one about their plans for the night. Then Tom suddenly remembered that Huck might come that very evening and give the signal. The possibility drained much of the excitement from his expectations. Even so, he couldn't bear to miss the fun at Widow Douglas's. Why should he miss it, he reasoned? The signal hadn't come last night, so why was it any more likely tonight? The evening's guaranteed pleasures outweighed the uncertain treasure. Like a boy, he decided to follow the stronger temptation and forbid himself to think about the money box again that day.

Three miles downstream from town, the ferry stopped and tied up at the entrance to a wooded hollow. Everyone poured ashore, and soon shouts and laughter echoed through the forest and over the rocky heights. They tried every possible way of getting hot and tired. Eventually the wanderers drifted back to camp with formidable appetites, and the good food began to disappear. After eating, they enjoyed a refreshing spell of rest and conversation beneath the spreading oaks. At last someone called:

“Who's ready to visit the cave?”

They all were. Bundles of candles were brought out, and everyone immediately raced up the hill. The cave entrance lay partway up the slope, an opening shaped like the letter A. Its heavy oak door stood unlocked. Inside was a small chamber as cold as an icehouse, with natural walls of solid limestone beaded with chilly moisture. Standing in that deep darkness and looking out at the sunlit green valley felt mysterious and romantic. But the wonder soon wore off, and the roughhousing resumed. Whenever someone lit a candle, everyone rushed at its owner. A struggle followed, with a valiant attempt at defense, but the candle was soon knocked away or blown out, provoking delighted laughter and another chase. Everything ends eventually, though. Before long they formed a procession and filed down the steep slope of the main passage, their flickering line of candles faintly lighting the towering rock walls almost to where they met sixty feet above. The passage was only eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps, other high and even narrower cracks branched away on either side, for McDougal's cave was an immense maze of winding corridors that joined one another, separated again, and led nowhere.

At noon on Saturday I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning powders to make smoke, waving his hands, and muttering nonsense as vigorously as ever. But he looked fairly discouraged: naturally, he hadn't managed to make that well produce so much as a sweat. Finally I asked:

“How are things looking now, partner?”

“At this moment I am testing the strongest spell known to the great masters of magic in the East. If it fails, nothing can help. Be quiet until I finish.”

This time he produced enough smoke to darken the whole area. The hermits must have found it unpleasant, since the wind blew their way and carried thick, rolling clouds down over their caves. He poured out words just as thickly, twisting his body and chopping at the air with his hands in an extraordinary fashion. After twenty minutes he collapsed, panting and nearly exhausted. Just then the abbot arrived with several hundred monks and nuns, followed by a crowd of pilgrims and enough abandoned children to cover a couple of acres. The tremendous smoke had drawn them all, and they were wildly excited. The abbot anxiously asked what had happened. Merlin replied:

“If any human effort could undo the spell that holds back this water, my latest attempt would have succeeded. It has failed. Now I know my fear was justified: the well is under the spell of the mightiest spirit known to Eastern magicians, whose name no one can speak and survive. No person alive, or yet to be born, can discover the secret of that spell, and without the secret no one can break it. The water will never run again, good Father. I have done everything a man can do. Let me leave.”

Naturally, the abbot was deeply alarmed. He turned to me, his face showing his dismay, and asked:

“You heard him. Is it true?”

“Some of it.”

“Then not everything! Which part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has cast a spell on the well.”

“By God's wounds, we're ruined!”

“Perhaps.”

“But not for certain? You mean there's still a chance?”

“Exactly.”

“Then you also mean that when he says no one can break the spell—”

“Yes. When he says that, he's saying something that isn't necessarily true. Under certain conditions, an attempt to break it might have a chance of succeeding—a small chance, that is, a very slight one.”

Many years back I became closely acquainted with a Mr. William Legrand. Descended from an old Huguenot family, he had formerly possessed wealth, but repeated misfortunes had brought him to poverty. To escape the humiliation attendant upon these reverses, he departed from New Orleans, his ancestral city, and settled on Sullivan's Island, near Charleston in South Carolina.

It is a most peculiar island, composed almost entirely of sea sand and extending about three miles in length. Nowhere is it more than a quarter-mile broad. A barely discernible creek divides it from the mainland, seeping through a waste of mud and reeds much frequented by marsh hens. Its plant life, as one would expect, is sparse, or at any rate stunted. Trees of considerable size are nowhere visible. At the western end, near Fort Moultrie and a handful of wretched timber houses occupied in summer by those escaping Charleston's dust and fever, the spiky palmetto does indeed grow. Apart from that western point and a strip of firm white beach along the ocean, however, thick growths of sweet myrtle cover the entire island—the very shrub so highly valued by English gardeners. Here it frequently rises fifteen or twenty feet, forming an almost impassable thicket and filling the air with its perfume.

Deep within this thicket, near the eastern, more secluded extremity of the island, Legrand had erected a little hut. He was living there when chance first brought us together. Our acquaintance quickly became friendship, for the solitary man possessed much to awaken regard and interest. I discovered that he was well schooled and endowed with uncommon mental abilities, though afflicted by dislike of mankind and contrary shifts between exuberance and gloom. He owned numerous books but seldom consulted them. His principal diversions were shooting and fishing, or wandering the shore and the myrtle groves in search of shells and insect specimens; his collection of insects was one a Swammerdamm might have coveted. An elderly negro named Jupiter usually joined these expeditions. He had received his freedom before the family's misfortunes, yet neither threats nor inducements could persuade him to surrender what he regarded as his privilege of following his young “Massa Will” wherever he went. It is quite possible that Legrand's relations, believing his mind somewhat disordered, had deliberately encouraged this stubbornness in Jupiter so that the wanderer might remain under watch and protection.
